questions.q: How does Scruton say a healthy society should be built?
a: From the bottom up, starting with its people
From the top down, under a strong leader
Around a single ruling political party
By leaving everything to the free market
questions.why: Lesson one says conservatives believe society should grow from its people toward their representatives, not be ruled from above.

questions.q: What does Scruton say is lost when a society abandons its history and values?
a: The shared bond that holds people together
The efficiency of its government agencies
Its ability to trade with other nations
The loyalty of its youngest citizens
questions.why: Lesson one warns that without a moral compass and shared history, a society becomes easier to divide and conquer.

questions.q: Why does Scruton oppose state ownership of institutions and businesses?
a: It puts dangerous amounts of power in a few hands
It makes goods too expensive for the poor
It discourages people from starting families
It weakens the country's military strength
questions.why: Lesson two calls central ownership utopian and warns that concentrating so much power is dangerous.

questions.q: Instead of closing private schools and clubs, what does Scruton recommend?
a: Opening them up so more people can benefit
Taxing them heavily until they disappear
Reserving them for government officials
Letting each one set its own rules
questions.why: Lesson two says the fix is to make elite institutions accessible to the masses rather than shut them down.

questions.q: How does Scruton describe healthy nationalism?
a: A family-like attachment to your country and its people
A belief that your nation should rule others
A rejection of all foreign goods and ideas
Loyalty to a political party above the nation
questions.why: Lesson three compares a nation to a family and defines nationalism as affection and belonging, not blind obedience.
